scenes.text: What if you did not drink any water for three days? Not a sip. Sounds simple, but your body would start to struggle very fast. How long can a person really last? And what happens inside you hour by hour? Let us find out, based on what doctors know. This is for learning, not medical advice.

First, why is water so important? About sixty percent of an adult body is water. It is in your blood, your brain, your muscles and even your bones. Your body uses water to carry food to your cells, to remove waste, and to keep your temperature steady.

And you lose water all the time. You lose it when you sweat, when you pass urine, and even when you simply breathe out. In total, an average person loses around two to three litres every day. So the water has to be replaced again and again.

In the first few hours, you feel thirsty. Thirst is your brain's alarm. When the amount of water in your blood drops even a little, special sensors tell your brain, and your mouth feels dry. Your urine also becomes darker and less in quantity.

By the end of the first day, many people feel a headache, tiredness and trouble focusing. Even mild dehydration can lower your mood and your attention. Studies show that losing just one or two percent of body water can make thinking harder.
Next, your blood becomes a little thicker, because it has less water in it. Your heart has to work harder to pump it, so your heartbeat can get faster. When you stand up quickly, you may feel dizzy.

Your kidneys now try to save every drop. They make very little urine, and it becomes strong and dark. Without enough water, waste builds up, and over time the kidneys can be damaged. Kidney stones also become more likely.
Your skin also shows it. It becomes dry and less stretchy, and your lips crack. Doctors sometimes pinch the skin on the back of the hand. If it goes back slowly, that is a sign of dehydration.

On the second day, things get serious. Weakness, muscle cramps, confusion and a very dry mouth are common. Without water, your body also cannot cool itself well, because sweating needs water. In hot weather, this is very dangerous.

Your brain feels it strongly. Brain cells need a steady balance of water and salts. When that balance is off, you may feel confused, irritable or sleepy. In severe cases, people can even faint or have seizures.

By the third day, a person can be in real danger. Very low blood pressure, a rapid pulse, almost no urine and extreme weakness are warning signs. This is a medical emergency, and the person needs urgent help from a doctor.

So how long can a person survive without water? The common idea is about three days, but there is no fixed number. It depends on the heat, on how active you are, and on your health. In very hot weather it can be much shorter, and in cool, calm conditions, it can be a bit longer.

Here is something surprising. A person can live for weeks without food, but only days without water. That is why in any emergency, water comes first. Water is simply more urgent than food for your body.

Now, some myths. Many people say you must drink exactly eight glasses a day. But the real need depends on you, your weather and your work. Another myth is that only water counts. In fact, tea, milk, fruits and vegetables also add to your water. And drinking too much, too fast, is also not good.

So how much do you really need? Many health bodies suggest about two to three litres of total fluids a day for adults, including water from food. You need more in summer, when you exercise, or when you are sick. Ask your doctor for your own number.

How can you tell if you need water? Look at your urine colour. Pale yellow usually means good. Dark yellow means you need more. Also watch for thirst, headaches and a dry mouth. Do not wait until you feel very thirsty.

Some easy habits can help. Keep a bottle near you. Drink a glass after waking up. Eat water-rich foods like cucumber, watermelon and oranges. And take small sips regularly, instead of gulping a lot at once.

If someone has been vomiting, has diarrhoea, a fever, or cannot keep fluids down, dehydration can happen quickly. Babies and older people are at higher risk. In that case, please talk to a doctor soon. Oral rehydration solution can help, but get advice.

So the lesson is clear. Water is not a luxury, it is the base of everything your body does. You do not need to be perfect. Just drink regularly, listen to your thirst, and keep an eye on your urine colour.
